title: Diffusion and Flow-based Copulas: Forgetting and Remembering Dependencies
claim: Two processes progressively forget dependencies while preserving marginals, and each yields a distinct way to learn, evaluate and sample the model.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right time frames, formulas in side boxes
description: Two stacked, color-coded panels. The top green panel is titled 'Classification-Diffusion Copula'. It shows five tilted density heatmaps at t=0.00 to 0.32. Green noisy SDE trajectories run across them as structure turns into uniform noise. Two arrows lead to rounded boxes on the right. One gives a density ratio of class probabilities for one-call density evaluation. The other gives a score-based formula for sample generation. A band between the panels reads 'Dependent copula → Only dependence is forgotten → Independent copula' with black arrows. The bottom blue panel is titled 'Reflection Copula'. It shows the same frames with straight blue reflecting particle paths. A large arrow leads to a box with the velocity predictor v(u,t) and the sampling recipe from uniform noise. Bold titles and the colored trajectories draw the eye first.
caption: Overview of proposed copula models. We design forward processes to forget inter-variable dependencies but preserve dimension-wise marginals. Our classification-diffusion copula and reflection copula learn by remembering the forgotten dependencies of these processes.
abstract: Copulas are a fundamental tool for modelling multivariate dependencies in data, forming the method of choice in diverse fields and applications. However, the adoption of existing models for multimodal and high-dimensional dependencies is hindered by restrictive assumptions and poor scaling. In this work, we present methods for modelling copulas based on the principles of diffusions and flows. We design two processes that progressively forget inter-variable dependencies while leaving dimension-wise distributions unaffected, provably defining valid copulas at all times. We show how to obtain copula models by learning to remember the forgotten dependencies from each process, theoretically recovering the true copula at optimality. The first instantiation of our framework focuses on direct density estimation, while the second specialises in expedient sampling. Empirically, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed methods over state-of-the-art copula approaches in modelling complex and high-dimensional dependencies from scientific datasets and images. Our work enhances the representational power of copula models, empowering applications and paving the way for their adoption on larger scales and more challenging domains.
